title: Vietnamese Spring Rolls
subtitle: fresh rice paper rolls with prawns, noodles, and dipping sauce
excerpt: Vietnamese fresh spring rolls (goi cuon) are not fried -- they are wrapped in soft rice paper with prawns, rice noodles, and fresh herbs. The result is light and refreshing. The nuoc cham dipping sauce, sharp with lime and fish sauce, ties everything together.
sourceNotes: Goi cuon (literally salad rolls) are a Vietnamese fresh roll distinct from the fried spring rolls more common in Chinese-influenced cuisines. They are associated with the south of Vietnam, particularly the Mekong Delta region. The rolls are served at room temperature and are popular as a light meal or starter.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dipping sauce can be made a day ahead. Rolls must be assembled to order -- they dry out quickly.

content.text: Fresh spring rolls are an assembly job, not a cooking job. Get all the fillings ready before you start rolling -- once you have a wet rice paper in your hands, you need to work quickly. Keep the filling compact and the rolls tight. A loose roll falls apart when you pick it up.

items.prepNote: use 100g rice vermicelli noodles -- cook, drain, and cool
finely shredded -- or use lettuce leaves
use 16 rice paper wrappers -- dip each in warm water for 10 seconds until pliable
use lime juice -- for the dipping sauce
juice of 1 lime -- for the dipping sauce

content.text: Prepare all the fillings: cook and drain the vermicelli noodles. Shred the cabbage and cut the carrot into matchsticks. Arrange everything in bowls ready to assemble.
Make the dipping sauce: mix the fish sauce, lime juice, honey, chilli flakes, and 2 tablespoons of water. Taste -- it should be salty, sour, and mildly sweet.
Fill a wide bowl with warm water. Dip one rice paper wrapper into the water for 10 seconds. It should feel soft and pliable but not torn. Lay flat on a damp clean surface.
Place 2 or 3 prawn halves in a horizontal line across the middle. Top with a small amount of noodles, shredded cabbage, carrot, and spring onion.
Fold the sides in, then roll from the bottom upward, pulling firmly to make a tight roll. Repeat.
Serve immediately with the dipping sauce. Rice paper dries out and stiffens if left uncovered.

items.cause: Over-soaked in water, or filling too large
items.fix: Dip the rice paper for exactly 10 seconds -- it continues to soften as you fill and roll it. Keep the filling small and compact. Roll firmly. If the paper tears, it cannot be salvaged -- start with a fresh one.

content.text: Goi cuon are a southern Vietnamese speciality. They are sold at markets and in cafes throughout Ho Chi Minh City. The rolls are lighter and fresher than fried spring rolls. Each roll should be neat and compact. The dipping sauce (nuoc cham) is the essential partner -- without it, the rolls taste flat.
